# Clinical Findings

The clinical spectrum includes cryptic infection, localized cutaneous disease (CL), and disseminated infection (DCL, MCL, and VL).

## <mark>Cutaneous Leishmaniasis</mark>

<mark>Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) constitutes 50% to 75% of all incident cases and is the mildest form of the disease.</mark> <mark>It can be caused by any *Leishmania* species.</mark> <mark>Most cases heal spontaneously within 1 year and are classified as acute CL.</mark> <mark>Disease lasting more than 1 year is termed chronic CL (CCL).</mark>

### <mark>Old World Cutaneous Leishmaniasis</mark>

<mark>Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis (OWCL), also known as Aleppo boil, Baghdad boil, Oriental sore, *leishmaniasis tropica*, Biskra button, Delhi boil, Bouton d'orient, Lahore sore, rose of Jericho, Kandahar sore, or "the little sister," is caused mainly by *L.</mark> <mark>major*, *L.</mark> <mark>tropica*, and *L.</mark> <mark>aethiopica*, and to a lesser extent by *L.</mark> <mark>infantum*.</mark> <mark>Two major types are recognized.</mark>

#### <mark>Moist or Rural Type</mark>

<mark>The moist or rural type is classically caused by *L.</mark> <mark>major* and is characterized by:</mark>
- <mark>Multiple lesions</mark>
- <mark>Short incubation period (1 week to 3 months)</mark>
- <mark>Rapid and mild clinical course</mark>
- <mark>Good response to therapy</mark>

<mark>Rodents are the primary reservoirs.</mark> <mark>After bites from infected sand flies, one or more (up to 100) insect bite–like lesions appear, typically on exposed areas such as the face, arms, and legs.</mark> <mark>Most resolve within 1–2 weeks; only a few progress to typical CL.</mark> <mark>These evolving lesions are painless and usually heal within 6 months, leaving atrophic scars.</mark>

#### <mark>Dry or Urban Type</mark>

<mark>The dry or urban type is classically caused by *L.</mark> <mark>tropica* and is characterized by:</mark>
- <mark>Longer incubation period and disease duration (approximately twice as long as the moist type)</mark>
- <mark>Poorer response to therapy</mark>
- <mark>Anthroponotic transmission (human-to-human via sand flies)</mark>
- <mark>Potential for persistence, progression, recurrence, and visceralization</mark>

<mark>A single "dry" ulcer, typically on the face, is characteristic.</mark>

<mark>These two types may coexist in the same patient.</mark> *L. <mark>aethiopica* may cause a similar cutaneous disease but carries a higher risk of progressing to diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL).</mark> *L. <mark>infantum*, the primary cause of Mediterranean visceral leishmaniasis in children, can cause a self-limited cutaneous disease in adults.</mark>

<mark>Species identification cannot be made based on clinical features alone and requires biochemical or molecular diagnostic methods.</mark>

### <mark>Morphologic Spectrum of OWCL</mark>

<mark>Lesions typically begin as erythematous papules that enlarge over several weeks into nodules or plaques.</mark> <mark>These often ulcerate and become crusted.</mark> <mark>The classic "volcanic" noduloulcerative lesion is painless and features:</mark>
- <mark>A crateriform ulcer</mark>
- <mark>A rolled border</mark>
- <mark>A necrotic base</mark>
- <mark>An adherent crust</mark>

<mark>Other clinical presentations include:</mark>
- <mark>Iceberg nodules</mark>
- <mark>Eczematoid</mark>
- <mark>Psoriasiform</mark>
- <mark>Erysipeloid</mark>
- <mark>Zosteriform</mark>
- <mark>Paronychial</mark>
- <mark>Chancriform</mark>
- Annular
- <mark>Palmoplantar</mark>
- <mark>Verrucous</mark>
- <mark>Keloidal lesions</mark>

<mark>Satellitosis, regional lymphadenopathy, localized lymphadenitis, and sporotrichoid lymphatic spread may also occur.</mark>

## Disseminated Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (DCL) in Immunosuppressed Patients

Immunosuppressed patients, particularly those with HIV infection, may develop disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL) without species-specific association. DCL typically follows a classical cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) lesion, with gradual development of non-ulcerated, parasite-laden nodules. These lesions have a predilection for exposed areas such as the extremities and face, where coalescence can result in leonine facies. Visceral involvement is absent. The disease follows a progressive or chronic course and is characterized by frequent relapse after treatment.

---

## <mark>Diagnosis of Cutaneous Leishmaniasis</mark>

<mark>Due to the potential toxicity of anti-leishmanial therapies, confirmation of diagnosis is essential.</mark>

<mark>Even when combining smear, histology, and culture, the parasite may not be detected in 10% to 20% of cases.</mark> <mark>Diagnostic challenges are more pronounced in New World leishmaniasis, especially in chronic lesions (>6 months duration).</mark> <mark>Therefore, using multiple diagnostic methods is recommended for optimal detection.</mark>

### <mark>Diagnostic Procedures</mark>

#### <mark>Skin Biopsy</mark>
<mark>A skin biopsy should be taken from the infiltrated margin of the lesion and divided into three parts for:</mark>
- <mark>Impression smear</mark>
- <mark>Histologic examination</mark>
- Culture

#### <mark>Smears</mark>
<mark>Smears can be obtained via fine needle aspiration or tissue scrapings.</mark> <mark>Success rates range from 50% to 80%.</mark>  
<mark>Procedure:</mark>
- <mark>Air-dry the sample</mark>
- <mark>Fix with methyl alcohol</mark>
- <mark>Stain with Giemsa</mark>
- <mark>Examine under oil immersion</mark>

<mark>Impression smears—prepared by gently pressing the biopsy specimen against a glass slide 2–5 times—offer higher sensitivity than routine histologic sections.</mark>

#### <mark>Histopathology</mark>
<mark>In both Old World (OW) and New World (NW) CL, early lesions show a dense, diffuse mixed inflammatory infiltrate composed mainly of histiocytes, with scattered multinucleated giant cells, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.</mark> <mark>Russell bodies (intracytoplasmic eosinophilic immunoglobulin deposits) may be present.</mark>

<mark>Features less commonly observed:</mark>
- <mark>Preservation of the papillary dermis (grenz zone)</mark>
- <mark>Presence of eosinophils and neutrophils</mark>
- <mark>Perineural inflammation</mark>

<mark>The hallmark of leishmaniasis—seen in approximately 70% of cases—is the presence of numerous **amastigotes** (Leishman-Donovan bodies) within histiocytes and extracellularly.</mark>  
- <mark>**Giemsa stain**: stains the parasite non-metachromatically; kinetoplast appears bright red.</mark>

<mark>As lesions evolve, amastigote numbers decrease, and histology resembles chronic cutaneous leishmaniasis (CCL), characterized by nodular or diffuse noncaseating tuberculoid granulomatous dermatitis.</mark>  
<mark>Other histologic findings:</mark>
- <mark>Variable epidermal hyperplasia and ulceration</mark>
- <mark>Scarring with marked loss of elastic fibers</mark>

<mark>In **DCL**, the infiltrate is diffuse, composed of vacuolated macrophages containing abundant intra- and extracellular amastigotes.</mark> <mark>The main differential diagnosis is **lepromatous leprosy**.</mark>

**Histologic Differential Diagnosis** (diseases with parasitized macrophages):
- **Histoplasmosis**: yeasts with surrounding halo
- **Granuloma inguinale**: safety-pin-like Donovan bodies
- **Rhinoscleroma**: Mikulicz cells
- Other considerations: blastomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, toxoplasmosis, trypanosomiasis

#### <mark>Other Diagnostic Procedures</mark>
<mark>**Laboratory animal inoculation (xenodiagnosis)** may be useful in cases with low parasite load when conventional methods fail.</mark>

# Transplantation Antigens and Graft-Versus-Host Disease (GVHD)

<mark>Transplantation antigens trigger immune responses leading to the targeting of host tissues, particularly epithelial tissues, for cytotoxic damage.</mark> <mark>The precise mechanism of lymphocyte-mediated injury remains unclear—whether it occurs primarily through direct cytotoxic molecules such as **granzyme** and **perforin**, through cytokine-mediated pathways, or via a combination of both.</mark> <mark>Epithelial cell death proceeds predominantly by **apoptosis**, with evidence supporting roles for both **T cell-mediated mechanisms** and **noncellular triggers**.</mark>

<mark>There is no consistent involvement of a single lymphocyte subset in mediating GVHD.</mark> <mark>Multiple epitopes on major and minor histocompatibility antigens can drive allostimulation, resulting in diverse populations of effector lymphocytes within target organs.</mark> <mark>For example, several cytotoxic **T-cell clones** have been isolated from the skin of a single patient.</mark> <mark>Both **CD4⁺** and **CD8⁺** T cells are capable of inducing epidermal damage.</mark> <mark>In murine models, the effector T-cell population responsible for cutaneous GVHD varies depending on the transplant strain combination, suggesting that each human donor-recipient pair may elicit a unique immune response involving different lymphocyte subsets.</mark> <mark>Nonetheless, clinical evidence supports a central role for **CD4⁺ T cells** in human GVHD pathogenesis.</mark> <mark>This immunologic diversity likely contributes to the variable clinical expression of GVHD, independent of MHC matching status.</mark>

<mark>Other immune cells also participate in GVHD.</mark> <mark>The presence of abundant **natural killer (NK) cells** in dermal and epidermal infiltrates during cutaneous GVHD suggests their recruitment following antigen-specific T-cell activation in target tissues.</mark> <mark>Additionally, increases in **mast cells** and **dermal dendrocytes** are observed in the superficial dermis during acute disease phases.</mark>

<mark>The reason for the frequent and early involvement of the skin in GVHD compared to liver or gastrointestinal manifestations remains unknown.</mark>

---

# Chronic Cutaneous Graft-Versus-Host Reaction after Allogeneic Stem Cell Transplantation

<mark>Chronic cutaneous GVHD closely resembles autoimmune disorders such as **lichen planus**, **scleroderma**, and **Sjögren's syndrome**, suggesting shared pathogenic mechanisms.</mark> <mark>Dysregulation of autoreactive immune components is thought to underlie these conditions.</mark> <mark>**Transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β)** plays a key role in the development of fibrotic skin and visceral changes seen in sclerodermoid GVHD, with studies showing that neutralizing antibodies against TGF-β can reverse fibrosis in mouse models.</mark>

<mark>Notably, in women with scleroderma, persistent **male fetal microchimerism** has been detected, prompting the hypothesis that a fetal anti-maternal immune reaction—akin to GVHD—may contribute to disease pathogenesis.</mark> <mark>In sclerodermatous skin, fibroblasts aberrantly express **MHC class II molecules** and produce excessive amounts of **type I collagen**, further supporting an immune-driven fibrotic process.</mark>

<mark>With the increasing use of **peripheral blood stem cell transplantation**, there may be a higher incidence of chronic GVHD, a consideration important for long-term patient management.</mark>

---

# Acute Cutaneous Graft-Versus-Host Reaction after Autologous and Syngeneic Marrow and Peripheral Stem Cell Transplantation

<mark>Evidence from rodent and human studies indicates that autoimmunity may develop against epitopes on **MHC class II molecules**.</mark> <mark>Since **IFN-γ** upregulates MHC class II expression—particularly on tumor cells—and **cyclosporine** promotes the expansion of MHC class II-reactive T cells, the combination of these factors with high-dose chemotherapy in autologous transplantation may enhance **GVH-like cutaneous reactions**.</mark> <mark>This phenomenon might also contribute to a beneficial **graft-versus-tumor effect**, even in the absence of allogeneic immunity.</mark>

---

# CLINICAL FINDINGS

## History

A thorough patient history is essential in evaluating suspected GVHD. Key elements include:  
- Type of transplant (allogeneic, autologous, syngeneic)  
- Time elapsed since transplantation  
- Conditioning regimen used  
- Use of immunosuppressive agents (e.g., cyclosporine, tacrolimus)  
- Presence of prior acute GVHD  
- Donor-recipient HLA match status  
- Recent infections or drug exposures  

These factors help differentiate GVHD from other dermatoses and guide further diagnostic evaluation.

## <mark>Chronic Cutaneous Graft-Versus-Host Reaction After Allogeneic Transplantation</mark>

The lichenoid form of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) closely resembles lichen planus, characterized by erythematous to violaceous, polygonal, and variably keratotic papules that typically arise on flexor surfaces. <mark>Over time, some patients develop more widespread involvement.</mark> The lichenoid phase often resolves with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

The sclerodermoid phase closely mimics scleroderma, presenting with plaques of thickened skin that have a shiny, somewhat atrophic appearance, along with variable hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation. These plaques show erythema and progressive loss of the pilosebaceous apparatus. Clinical severity varies: some patients develop only a few sclerodermoid plaques and remain asymptomatic, while others progress to widespread disease associated with joint contractures, chronic cutaneous ischemia, erosions, alopecia, and a syndrome of general wasting. Recurrent bacterial skin infections are common, reflecting the underlying immunodeficiency that characterizes chronic GVHD. This immunocompromise predisposes patients to sepsis, a frequent cause of death.

The distinction between the lichenoid and sclerodermoid phases of chronic GVHD is not absolute. There is significant overlap between the two forms in many patients. Moreover, lichen planus-like eruptions can occur early after transplantation. Given the influence of immunomodulation and variability in histocompatibility on clinical presentation, rigid classification of GVHD phases based solely on time may not be clinically appropriate.

### Histopathology of Chronic Cutaneous Graft-Versus-Host Reaction after Allogeneic Transplantation

Histopathologic examination of lichenoid chronic GVHR may reveal fully developed features indistinguishable from lichen planus.

# <mark>GRAFT-VERSUS-HOST DISEASE</mark>

# <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

Acute cutaneous graft-versus-host reaction (GVHR) develops in 20 percent to 80 percent of patients undergoing allogeneic bone marrow transplantation, usually 10 to 30 days after infusion.  
<mark>Skin is the earliest and most frequent target.</mark> Liver and gastrointestinal involvement are also common; elevated total bilirubin levels and diarrhea can aid in establishing the diagnosis.  

Predisposing factors include mismatch in major histocompatibility complex (MHC) antigens, transplantation between unrelated individuals, older age, and certain prophylactic regimens.  

<mark>The eruptions of acute GVHR typically begin as faint, erythematous macules on any skin surface, sometimes with a perifollicular pattern in early stages, and may progress to erythroderma (later stages) or bullae (stage 4).</mark>  

<mark>Pathologic features of acute GVHR include a dermal lymphocytic infiltrate, basal layer vacuolar alteration, and epidermal cell necrosis at a frequency of at least four apoptotic bodies per linear millimeter of epidermis (grade 2).</mark>  

Chronic GVHR generally occurs more than 60 days after allogeneic marrow transplantation, with an incidence of approximately 25 percent. It is classified into lichenoid and sclerodermoid forms.  

Cutaneous eruptions resembling acute allogeneic GVHR can occur after autologous and syngeneic transplantation in up to 10 percent of patients.

The concept of lymphocyte recovery eruption is relevant in stem cell transplantation, as GVHRs often develop during peripheral lymphocyte recovery and reflect immunologic differences between donor and recipient or result from immunologic manipulation. Some histologically non-specific cutaneous eruptions in patients at risk for GVHD may represent lymphocyte recovery eruptions rather than true GVHR, since acute cutaneous GVHR requires cytotoxic targeting of the epidermis by donor-derived effector lymphocytes.

# EPIDEMIOLOGY AND INCIDENCE

Marrow-ablative regimens vary and commonly include combinations of cyclophosphamide, busulfan, total-body irradiation, methotrexate, and thiotepa.  

Acute cutaneous GVHR occurs in 20% to 80% of patients, typically 10 to 30 days after stem cell infusion. Risk factors include MHC antigen mismatch, unrelated donor transplantation, older age, and specific prophylactic regimens.  

Patients often receive high-dose cyclosporine at the time of transplantation to promote engraftment and reduce GVHD severity. Other strategies to prevent GVHD involve antibody-mediated depletion of putative effector T cells from the graft.

Chronic GVHD is divided into lichenoid and sclerodermoid subtypes. The lichenoid form usually precedes the sclerodermoid form, and both typically manifest beyond 60 days post-transplant. Some patients experience both types sequentially or simultaneously. Prior acute GVHD is the strongest predictor for developing chronic GVHD. The overall incidence of chronic cutaneous GVHD is about 25%. Rare cases have been reported following autologous transplantation.

Cutaneous eruptions mimicking acute allogeneic GVHR occur in up to 10% of patients after autologous or syngeneic transplants. Prospective studies on eruptions in peripheral blood stem cell transplant recipients are limited, but mild skin eruptions are observed coinciding with peripheral lymphocyte recovery.

## <mark>Treatment of Severe Nodular/Conglobate Acne</mark>

### <mark>High Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Oral isotretinoin** is strongly recommended as monotherapy for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne due to its superior efficacy compared to systemic antibiotics or topical therapy alone.</mark>

### <mark>Medium Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic antibiotics** in combination with the fixed-dose combination of **adapalene and benzoyl peroxide (BPO)**, or with **azelaic acid**, can be recommended for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne.</mark>

### <mark>Low Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic antibiotics** in combination with **adapalene** or **BPO** can be considered for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne.</mark>
- <mark>For females: **Hormonal anti-androgens** in combination with systemic antibiotics and topical treatments (excluding topical antibiotics) can be considered.</mark>
- <mark>For females: **Hormonal anti-androgens** in combination with a topical treatment (excluding antibiotics) can also be considered.</mark>

### <mark>Open Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>Due to insufficient evidence, no recommendation can be made for or against the use of **intense pulsed light (IPL)** or **laser therapy** in severe nodular/conglobate acne.</mark>
- <mark>Although **photodynamic therapy (PDT)** shows effectiveness, it cannot currently be recommended due to lack of standardized treatment protocols and concerns about acute adverse reactions.</mark>

### <mark>Negative Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Topical monotherapy** is not recommended for conglobate acne.</mark>
- <mark>**Oral antibiotics** are not recommended as monotherapy.</mark>
- <mark>**Oral anti-androgens** are not recommended as monotherapy.</mark>
- <mark>**Artificial UV radiation sources** are not recommended.</mark>
- <mark>**Visible light therapy** as monotherapy is not recommended.</mark>

---

## <mark>Choice of Topical vs. Systemic Treatment</mark>

<mark>There is limited evidence directly comparing topical and systemic therapies or evaluating the added benefit of combination therapy over topical treatment alone.</mark> <mark>Most studies compare topical antibiotic monotherapy with systemic antibiotic monotherapy.</mark>

<mark>In clinical practice, expert consensus supports that:</mark>
- <mark>Patients with **severe papulopustular acne** or **moderate nodular acne** achieve better outcomes with **systemic antibiotic plus topical treatment**, or with **systemic isotretinoin**.</mark>
- <mark>Involvement of the trunk is a key factor favoring systemic therapy.</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic treatments** are associated with better adherence and higher patient satisfaction, particularly in widespread disease.</mark>

---

## <mark>Additional Considerations</mark>

- <mark>**Isotretinoin** is highly effective in severe cases, supported by strong clinical experience despite limited controlled trial data specific to nodular/conglobate forms.</mark>
- <mark>Evidence for many treatment options was downgraded due to reliance on indirect data from studies of severe papulopustular acne, particularly when assessing nodule and cyst reduction.</mark>
- <mark>Prescribers should be mindful of the risk of **antibiotic resistance** when using systemic antibiotics.</mark>
- <mark>Systemic antibiotics such as **doxycycline** and **lymecycline** should be limited to a maximum treatment duration of **3 months**.</mark>
- <mark>In cases where higher-strength recommendations cannot be followed (due to cost, availability, licensing, or legal restrictions), lower-strength alternatives may be used as first-line therapy.</mark>

---

## Treatment of Papulopustular Acne

There is insufficient evidence to recommend laser or light-based therapies (other than blue light) for papulopustular acne due to lack of standardized protocols, clinical trial data, and real-world experience.

Systemic treatment with **isotretinoin** is recommended in severe cases based on high efficacy observed in clinical practice, although safety and tolerability data remain limited and insufficient for guiding recommendations independently.

# A Consensus-Based Practical and Daily Guide for the Treatment of Acne Patients

## Abstract

**Background**  
Many current guidelines provide detailed evidence-based recommendations for acne treatment.

**Objective**  
To create consensus-based, simple, easy-to-use algorithms for clinical acne treatment in daily office-based practice and to provide checklists to assist in determining why a patient may not have responded to treatment and what action to take.

**Methods**  
Existing treatment guidelines and consensus papers were reviewed. The information was extracted and simplified according to daily clinical practice needs using a consensus-based approach and based on the authors' clinical expertise.

**Results**  
Separate simple algorithms are presented for the treatment of:
- <mark>Predominant comedonal acne</mark>
- <mark>Predominant papulopustular acne</mark>
- <mark>Nodular/conglobate acne</mark>

- **Comedonal acne**: Initial treatment with topical retinoid, azelaic acid, or salicylic acid.
- **Papulopustular acne**: Fixed-combination topicals recommended, with therapy tailored to disease severity.
- **Nodular/conglobate acne**: Oral isotretinoin or fixed combinations plus oral antibiotics (in men); in women, these may be supplemented with oral anti-androgenic hormonal therapy.

Treatment response should be evaluated:
- **8 weeks** after initiation for comedonal or papulopustular acne
- **12 weeks** after initiation for nodular/conglobate acne

Once clear or almost clear, **maintenance therapy** with a topical retinoid or azelaic acid is recommended to prevent recurrence.

Reasons for lack of treatment response fall into five categories:
1. Disease progression  
2. Non-drug-related reasons  
3. Drug-related reasons  
4. Poor adherence  
5. Adverse events  

**Conclusion**  
This practical guide provides dermatologists with simple, clinically applicable treatment algorithms tailored to different acne types. The included checklists for evaluating treatment failure facilitate effective management in daily practice.

---

## Introduction

Acne is a chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit, commonly affecting adolescents and imposing a significant psychosocial and physical burden. The primary pathogenic factors include:
- Increased sebum production  
- Abnormal keratinization  
- Colonization by *Cutibacterium acnes* (formerly *Propionibacterium acnes*)  
- Inflammatory response mediated by innate immunity  

Due to this multifactorial pathophysiology, effective treatment typically requires combination therapy targeting multiple pathways.

Clinically, acne presents in various forms. This article focuses on three main types:
1. **Predominant comedonal facial acne**  
2. **Predominant papulopustular facial acne**  
3. **Nodular and/or conglobate acne** (affecting face, trunk, and upper limbs)

While numerous national and international guidelines offer evidence-based recommendations, there remains a need for simplified, practical tools that can be easily applied in routine clinical settings. 

This article presents:
- Consensus-based treatment algorithms for the three main acne types  
- Checklists to identify causes of treatment failure  
- Guidance on next steps when response is inadequate  

Special populations such as infants, adult women with hormonal acne, and syndromic acne are not addressed here.

---

## Methods

The treatment algorithms were developed by a panel of 17 acne experts. The process involved:
- Review of key international, evidence-based acne guidelines, including those from:
  - Global Alliance to Improve Outcomes in Acne  
  - European Dermatology Forum  
  - American Academy of Dermatology  
  - Asian expert groups  

The data from these sources were synthesized, simplified, and adapted to reflect real-world clinical practice through expert consensus and clinical experience. Recent literature was also considered to support recommendations.

---

## <mark>Results</mark>

### <mark>Treatment Algorithms</mark>

<mark>For ease of use in daily practice, separate algorithms are provided for:</mark>

#### <mark>1. Predominant Comedonal Acne</mark>
<mark>**First-line treatment:**</mark>
- <mark>Topical retinoid</mark>  
- <mark>Azelaic acid</mark>  
- <mark>Salicylic acid</mark>  

<mark>These agents normalize follicular keratinization and prevent comedone formation.</mark>

#### <mark>2. Predominant Papulopustular Acne</mark>
<mark>**Recommended:**</mark>
- <mark>Fixed-combination topical therapies (e.g., benzoyl peroxide + antibiotic, retinoid + benzoyl peroxide, or retinoid + antibiotic)</mark>  
- <mark>Therapy should be adjusted based on severity</mark>

<mark>Combination products improve efficacy and reduce antibiotic resistance risk.</mark>

#### <mark>3. Nodular/Conglobate Acne</mark>
<mark>**Treatment options:**</mark>
- <mark>**Oral isotretinoin** – first-line for severe nodular or conglobate acne</mark>  
- <mark>**Fixed combinations + oral antibiotics** – alternative in men if isotretinoin is contraindicated or declined</mark>  
- <mark>**In women**: Consider adding **oral anti-androgenic hormonal therapy** (e.g., combined oral contraceptives, spironolactone) as adjunctive treatment</mark>

### Evaluation of Treatment Response

Assessment should be performed using the **Global Evaluation Acne (GEA) scale**.

- **Clinical improvement**: Reduction of at least one to two grades on the GEA scale  
- **Timing of evaluation**:
  - **8 weeks** for comedonal and papulopustular acne  
  - **12 weeks** for nodular/conglobate acne  

### Maintenance Therapy

Once a patient is clear or almost clear:
- Initiate **maintenance therapy** with:
  - Topical retinoid  
  - Or azelaic acid  
- Purpose: Prevent recurrence by maintaining follicular patency and reducing inflammation

### Checklist: Causes of Treatment Failure

When a patient fails to respond, consider the following five categories:

1. **Disease progression**  
   - Natural course of acne may worsen before improving  
   - Consider escalation of therapy if progression occurs

2. **Non-drug-related reasons**  
   - Hormonal fluctuations (e.g., menstrual cycle, PCOS)  
   - Lifestyle factors (diet, stress, skincare practices)  
   - Cosmetic product use (comedogenic ingredients)

3. **Drug-related reasons**  
   - Inappropriate choice of agent for acne type/severity  
   - Suboptimal dosing or formulation  
   - Drug interactions

4. **Poor adherence**  
   - Common due to complex regimens, side effects, or lack of immediate results  
   - Simplify regimen, educate patient, and assess understanding

5. **Adverse events**  
   - Irritation, dryness, or allergic reactions may limit use  
   - Adjust formulation, frequency, or switch agents

For each identified cause, appropriate corrective actions should be taken, such as modifying treatment, improving patient education, or switching therapies.

## <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>

### <mark>History</mark>

The typical history is of a newly acquired, slowly expanding, persistent, and often scaly lesion of the skin. <mark>Over several weeks to months, the appearance of additional nearby lesions is suggestive of local spread and supports the diagnosis of HPV infection.</mark>

### Cutaneous Lesions

Warts are classified by their clinical location or morphology. The cutaneous manifestations of warts are varied, as illustrated in Figures 196-3 to 196-8.

**Common warts** (*verruca vulgaris*) are scaly, rough, spiny papules or nodules that can occur on any cutaneous surface. They most commonly appear as solitary or grouped lesions on the hands and fingers (see Figs. 196-3A to 196-5). These warts may also present in a **filiform** form (see Fig. 196-6) or as **cutaneous horns**.

**Flat warts** (*verruca plana*) are 1 to 4 mm, slightly elevated, flat-topped papules with minimal scale (see Fig. 196-8). They are most frequently found on the face, hands, and lower legs.

**Plantar and palmar warts** are thick, endophytic, and hyperkeratotic papules that may be painful under pressure (see Fig. 196-3B,C). After removal of the overlying keratin, punctate black dots—representing thrombosed capillaries within the papillary dermal papillae—may become visible. These are often referred to as "seeds."

# Guidance for the diagnosis of AGW

<mark>In terms of diagnosis, the key challenge is ensuring that anogenital warts (AGW) are correctly identified.</mark> <mark>AGW are typically diagnosed clinically based on their characteristic morphology and anogenital location.</mark> <mark>In most cases, diagnostic testing is not required when the lesions are typical in appearance.</mark>

## Clinical Evaluation

A thorough history and physical examination are essential for accurate diagnosis and effective management. The following elements should be included during the initial patient consultation:

### Patient History Checklist:
- **Symptoms**: Presence of itching, bleeding, discomfort, or pain
- **Duration**: Onset and progression of lesions
- **Number and location** of warts (e.g., penile, scrotal, vulvar, vaginal, cervical, perianal, anal)
- **Morphology**: Appearance (e.g., exophytic, papular, keratotic, flat)
- **Previous episodes** of AGW and history of recurrence
- **Prior treatments** used (type, duration, response, side effects)
- **Sexual history**: Number of partners, condom use, recent new partners
- **HPV vaccination status**
- **Immunocompromising conditions** (e.g., HIV infection, immunosuppressive therapy)
- **Psychosocial impact**: Emotional distress, anxiety, shame, effect on relationships or sexual activity

### Physical Examination:
- Inspection of external genitalia, perianal area, and adjacent skin under adequate lighting
- Use of a magnifying lens if necessary
- Application of 3–5% acetic acid (optional) to highlight subclinical lesions (though this is not routinely recommended due to low specificity)
- For women: speculum examination to assess vaginal and cervical involvement
- For men who have sex with men (MSM) or individuals with anal receptive intercourse: digital rectal examination and/or anoscopy to evaluate for internal anal warts

## Differential Diagnosis

Conditions that may mimic AGW include:
- **Pearly penile papules**
- **Hirsuties papillaris genitalis**
- **Sebaceous hyperplasia**
- **Molluscum contagiosum**
- **Condyloma lata** (syphilitic lesion – requires serological testing)
- **Squamous cell carcinoma** (especially in immunocompromised patients or long-standing lesions)
- **Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN)** or **anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN)**

Biopsy should be considered in cases of:
- Atypical appearance (e.g., pigmentation, ulceration, induration)
- Poor response to standard therapy
- Suspected malignancy
- Immunocompromised patients
- Perianal warts in children (to rule out sexual abuse)

## Role of Diagnostic Testing

- **HPV DNA testing** is not recommended for routine diagnosis of AGW, as it does not change management.
- **Acetic acid testing** has limited utility and may lead to false positives; its use is discouraged outside of specific settings such as colposcopy.
- **Serological tests** for syphilis should be performed if condyloma lata is suspected.
- **HIV testing** should be offered, particularly in patients with extensive, recurrent, or atypical warts.

## Patient Communication: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

To support patient understanding and reduce anxiety, physicians should address common concerns:

- **"Are anogenital warts caused by cancer-causing viruses?"**  
  No, most AGW are caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11, which do not cause cancer.

- **"Can I pass this to my partner?"**  
  Yes, HPV can be transmitted through skin-to-skin contact, even without visible warts.

- **"Will I always have this?"**  
  Most people clear the infection within months to a couple of years. Recurrences are common but tend to decrease over time.

- **"Should my partner be examined?"**  
  Routine screening of asymptomatic partners is not recommended, but they should be informed so they can seek care if symptoms develop.

- **"Does this mean my partner was unfaithful?"**  
  Not necessarily. HPV can remain dormant for months or years before causing symptoms.

- **"Can I still have sex?"**  
  Yes, but using condoms may reduce transmission risk (though they do not fully protect due to uncovered skin areas).

This structured approach to diagnosis ensures accurate identification of AGW, appropriate exclusion of mimicking conditions, and effective patient counseling.

## <mark>HPV Vaccination and Anogenital Warts</mark>

- Smoking is associated with persistence of anogenital HPV infection. Although there is no evidence that smoking cessation improves wart treatment outcomes, there is a clear individual and public health rationale for advising smoking cessation. (1C)

- <mark>**Gardasil®** and **Gardasil9®** (both by MSD Vaccins) provide durable protection against HPV genotypes 6 and 11, which cause the majority of anogenital warts.</mark>

- <mark>A recent trial suggested a possible benefit of using the vaccine in combination with topical **imiquimod** or **podophyllotoxin** for treatment or prevention of recurrence of genital warts, but this remains unconfirmed.</mark>

- There is no evidence of benefit from vaccination in individuals with HPV infection but no clinical disease.

- <mark>Vaccination prior to sexual debut maximizes protective benefits.</mark>

- HPV vaccination strategies vary by country.

- <mark>Substantial reductions in genital wart incidence have been observed in young women and heterosexual men in **Australia** following the introduction of **Gardasil®** vaccination in schoolgirls.</mark>

- <mark>A reduction in genital warts was also observed in women and heterosexual men aged 15–19 in the **UK** following the introduction of the **bivalent vaccine Cervarix®** (GlaxoSmithKline), despite its lack of coverage for HPV 6 and 11, suggesting possible cross-protection or herd effects.</mark>

# 2012 European guideline for the management of anogenital warts

## Abstract

<mark>**Background**</mark>  
<mark>Although new HPV vaccines have been developed and are in the process of implementation, anogenital warts remain a very frequent problem in clinical practice.</mark>

**Objective**  
To update previously published European guidelines for the management of anogenital warts.

**Methods**  
A systematic review of randomized controlled trials for anogenital warts was conducted. The primary data were analyzed and collated, and the findings were formulated into a clinical guideline. The draft was reviewed by the IUSTI Europe Editorial Board and made available online for public comment; feedback was incorporated into the final version.

**Results**  
The data confirm that only surgical therapies achieve primary clearance rates approaching 100%. Recurrences—包括 previously treated sites or new lesions—occur after all treatments, with recurrence rates often 20–30% or higher. All treatment modalities are associated with local skin reactions such as itching, burning, erosions, and pain.

**Conclusions**  
Physicians managing patients with genital warts should develop individualized treatment algorithms based on local practices and guidelines. Patient management should include clinical review at least every 4 weeks, with a change in therapy if there is an inadequate response. Patients with first-episode warts should be offered screening for other sexually transmitted infections. Management must also include partner notification and health promotion.

---

## <mark>Aetiology and transmission</mark>

<mark>Anogenital warts (also known as genital warts, condylomata acuminata, or condylomas) are benign proliferative lesions caused primarily by human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11, which are detected in >90% of cases.</mark> <mark>Co-infection with high-risk HPV types, such as HPV 16, is common.</mark> <mark>Genital warts are transmitted sexually, with an estimated transmission rate of approximately 60% between untreated sexual partners.</mark>

This guideline was developed on behalf of:
- The European Branch of the International Union against Sexually Transmitted Infections (IUSTI Europe)
- The European Dermatology Federation (EDF)
- The Union of European Medical Specialists (UEMS)

---

## Clinical features

### Symptoms

Most patients are asymptomatic aside from the visible presence of lesions. When symptoms occur, they may include itching, bleeding, fissuring, or dyspareunia.

### Physical signs

Lesions typically appear at sites subject to trauma during intercourse. They may be solitary, but multiple lesions (usually 5–15) measuring 1–5 mm in diameter are more common. Warts can coalesce into larger plaques, particularly in immunosuppressed individuals or those with diabetes.

In uncircumcised men, the preputial cavity—including the glans penis, coronal sulcus, frenulum, and inner foreskin—is most frequently affected. In circumcised men, the penile shaft is more commonly involved. Other sites include the urethral meatus, pubis, scrotum, groin, perineum, perianal area, and anal canal.

In women, warts may occur on the fourchette, labia minora, labia majora, pubis, clitoris, urethral meatus, perineum, perianal region, anal canal, introitus, vagina, and ectocervix.

Intra-anal warts are most frequently seen in individuals who practice receptive anal intercourse, though they can occur without it. Warts are rarely found proximal to the dentate line.

Anogenital warts vary in color from pink or salmon red to white, greyish-white, or various shades of brown (pigmented lesions). Pigmentation is more commonly observed on the labia majora, penile shaft, pubis, groin, perineum, and perianal area.

---

## Complications

### Physical and psychosexual implications

Anogenital warts are often perceived as disfiguring and can significantly affect sexual well-being. Patients may experience anxiety, guilt, anger, and reduced self-esteem. Common concerns include potential effects on fertility and cancer risk.

### Pre-cancer and cancer

Premalignant conditions—such as vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN), anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN), and penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN)—as well as invasive cancers (vulval, anal, and penile) may coexist with anogenital warts, develop within them, or be initially misdiagnosed as warts. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for such conditions, especially in persistent, atypical, or treatment-resistant lesions.

# <mark>PATHOGENESIS</mark>

<mark>Mechanisms have been extensively studied in herpes-associated erythema multiforme (EM).</mark> <mark>It remains unclear whether similar pathophysiological processes apply to EM caused by other triggers.</mark>

Complete infectious herpes simplex virus (HSV) has never been isolated from lesions of herpes-associated EM. <mark>However, HSV DNA fragments—always including the viral polymerase (Pol) gene—have been detected in EM lesions using PCR assays.</mark> <mark>These fragments are found primarily in basal keratinocytes and the lower spinous layers of the epidermis.</mark> <mark>The HSV Pol protein is expressed in epidermal cells, leading to recruitment of HSV-specific T cells, including cytotoxic T lymphocytes.</mark> <mark>This virus-specific immune response is followed by a broader, non-specific inflammatory reaction mediated by autoreactive T cells.</mark> <mark>The resulting cytokine release contributes to the delayed hypersensitivity-like histopathology characteristic of EM lesions.</mark>

<mark>HSV is transiently present in the bloodstream around the time of symptomatic herpes recurrence.</mark> If keratinocytes were directly infected via hematogenous spread, widespread cutaneous herpes would be expected rather than the localized lesions seen in EM. <mark>Instead, evidence suggests that HSV DNA is transported to the skin by monocytes, macrophages, and particularly CD34⁺ Langerhans cell progenitors that express the cutaneous lymphocyte-associated antigen (CLA), a skin-homing receptor.</mark> <mark>Upregulation of adhesion molecules enhances the binding of these HSV-carrying mononuclear cells to vascular endothelium.</mark> <mark>Increased expression of HLA class I and adhesion molecules on endothelial cells likely contributes to the dermal inflammation observed in EM.</mark>

<mark>Upon reaching the epidermis, these cells transfer the viral Pol gene to keratinocytes.</mark> <mark>While the genetic material may persist for several months, Pol protein expression is transient, lasting only a few days—consistent with the self-limited nature of EM lesions.</mark>

<mark>Variations in the efficiency of viral DNA fragmentation, elevated levels of circulating CD34⁺ cells, or an exaggerated immune response to the Pol protein may explain why only a small subset of individuals with recurrent herpes develop EM.</mark>

# CLINICAL FINDINGS

Diagnosis begins with clinical suspicion for EM based on characteristic features. Skin biopsy and laboratory tests are primarily helpful when the diagnosis is uncertain.

The second step is to assess the need for hospitalization, particularly in cases of EM major (EMM) with oral involvement impairing feeding, suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), or severe systemic symptoms.

The third step involves identifying the underlying cause—most commonly recurrent herpes simplex infection, Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection, or other triggers—through patient history, chest imaging, or serological testing.

# History

Prodromal symptoms are typically absent. When present, they are mild and resemble an upper respiratory tract infection (e.g., cough, rhinitis, low-grade fever).

In EMM, fever exceeding 38.5°C (101.3°F) occurs in approximately one-third of cases.

A history of prior EM episodes is reported in at least one-third of patients and supports the diagnosis. A detailed review of events within the preceding three weeks should focus on potential triggers, especially recurrent herpes outbreaks.

# Cutaneous Lesions

The rash appears suddenly. In most patients, all lesions develop within three days, although some may experience successive crops during a single episode.

The number of lesions varies widely—from just a few to hundreds. They are typically symmetric and acral, predominantly affecting the extensor surfaces of the extremities (hands, feet, elbows, knees), face, and neck. Involvement of the thighs, buttocks, and trunk is less common.

# <mark>ETIOLOGY</mark>

<mark>Most cases of erythema multiforme (EM) are related to infections.</mark> <mark>Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is definitively the most common cause, particularly in recurrent cases.</mark> <mark>The causal relationship between HSV and EM is well established through clinical experience, epidemiology, detection of HSV DNA in EM lesions, and the prevention of EM with antiviral suppression of HSV recurrences.</mark> <mark>A clinical link with herpes can be identified in approximately half of EM cases.</mark> <mark>Additionally, 10% to 40% of cases without apparent herpes symptoms are also found to be herpes-related, as HSV DNA is detectable in EM lesions by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing.</mark> <mark>EM eruptions typically begin around 7 days after a herpes recurrence, although the interval can be shorter.</mark> <mark>Not every symptomatic HSV recurrence leads to EM, and EM can even follow asymptomatic HSV reactivation, making the connection easy to overlook by both patients and clinicians.</mark> <mark>HSV-1 is the primary subtype involved, though HSV-2 can also trigger EM; the relative frequency reflects general HSV subtype prevalence in the population.</mark>

<mark>*Mycoplasma pneumoniae* is the second major cause of EM and may be the leading cause in children.</mark> <mark>EM associated with *M.</mark> <mark>pneumoniae* often presents with atypical and more severe features compared to HSV-related cases.</mark> <mark>Establishing the link can be challenging, as clinical and radiological signs of pneumonia may be mild, and direct detection of *M.</mark> <mark>pneumoniae* is uncommon.</mark> <mark>PCR testing of throat swabs offers the highest sensitivity.</mark> <mark>Serologically, the diagnosis is supported by the presence of immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies or a greater than twofold rise in immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies to *M.</mark> <mark>pneumoniae*.</mark> <mark>EM related to *M.</mark> <mark>pneumoniae* can recur.</mark>

Other infectious agents have been occasionally linked to EM in isolated cases or small series, but evidence for causality remains circumstantial. These include orf virus, varicella-zoster virus, parvovirus B19, hepatitis B and C viruses, and infectious mononucleosis, as well as various bacterial and viral infections. Immunizations have also been reported as potential triggers, particularly in children.

Drug-induced EM with mucous membrane involvement is rare. It remains uncertain whether such eruptions represent true EM or mimics such as annular urticaria or maculopapular drug eruptions with target-like lesions.

Idiopathic EM refers to cases where no HSV infection or other identifiable cause is found. These are relatively common in routine practice. <mark>However, HSV DNA has been detected by PCR in up to 40% of recurrent "idiopathic" cases.</mark> <mark>Some of these respond to prophylactic antiviral therapy, suggesting asymptomatic HSV reactivation as the trigger, while others do not, indicating possible alternative mechanisms.</mark>

EM-like dermatitis can also arise from contact sensitization. Despite clinical and histopathological similarities, these eruptions should be considered mimics of EM rather than true EM.

# <mark>PATHOGENESIS</mark>

<mark>The pathogenesis of EM has been most thoroughly studied in herpes-associated cases.</mark> <mark>It is unclear whether the same mechanisms apply to EM caused by other agents.</mark>

<mark>Infectious HSV has never been isolated from EM lesions.</mark> <mark>However, HSV DNA fragments—consistently including the viral polymerase (Pol) gene—have been detected in lesional keratinocytes using PCR.</mark> <mark>These fragments are localized primarily in basal and lower spinous layer keratinocytes, where the HSV Pol protein is also expressed.</mark> <mark>This leads to recruitment of HSV-specific T cells, including cytotoxic T cells.</mark> <mark>The initial virus-specific immune response is followed by a broader, non-specific inflammatory reaction mediated by autoreactive T cells.</mark>

# <mark>HERPES SIMPLEX</mark>

# <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

<mark>Herpes simplex viruses (HSVs) are common human DNA viral pathogens that intermittently re-activate.</mark> After replication in the skin or mucosa, the virus infects local nerve endings and ascends to the ganglia, where it establishes latency until re-activation.

There are two types of HSV: HSV-1 and HSV-2. HSV-1 is primarily associated with orofacial infections, while HSV-2 typically causes genital infections. However, both types can infect oral and genital areas and cause acute and recurrent disease.

Most adults are seropositive for HSV-1, with the majority of infections acquired during childhood. Approximately one-fourth of adults in the United States are infected with HSV-2, with acquisition closely linked to sexual activity.

Most primary HSV infections are asymptomatic or unrecognized, though they can occasionally cause severe disease. Similarly, most recurrences are asymptomatic—referred to as asymptomatic shedding—and this is the primary mode of transmission.

Genital herpes is the most prevalent sexually transmitted infection worldwide and the leading cause of ulcerative genital disease. It is also a significant risk factor for the acquisition and transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

HSV can also cause infections of the eye (e.g., keratitis), central nervous system (e.g., encephalitis), and neonatal herpes. Defects in cellular immunity increase the risk of severe, disseminated, or chronic HSV infections.

Diagnosis is based on viral culture, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and serology, depending on the clinical context.

Treatment involves antiviral agents such as **acyclovir**, **valacyclovir**, or **famciclovir**. Regimens and dosages vary by clinical presentation. Antiviral resistance is rare except in immunocompromised individuals.

After DNA replication, the expression of more than 60 "late" HSV-2 genes occurs. <mark>These genes encode virion structural components and proteins required for proper viral assembly.</mark>

# <mark>PATHOGENESIS</mark>

<mark>In vivo, HSV infection progresses through three stages: acute infection, establishment and maintenance of latency, and re-activation.</mark>

<mark>During acute infection, the virus replicates at the site of inoculation on mucocutaneous surfaces, producing primary lesions.</mark> <mark>Virus particles then spread to sensory nerve terminals and undergo retrograde axonal transport to neuronal nuclei in regional sensory ganglia.</mark>

<mark>In a subset of infected neurons, a latent infection is established.</mark> <mark>During latency, viral DNA persists as an episome, and gene expression is highly restricted—only one viral transcript, the latency-associated transcript (LAT), is abundantly expressed.</mark>

<mark>In the final stage, re-activation occurs, leading to viral replication and anterograde axonal transport of newly assembled virions to peripheral sites, often near the original site of entry.</mark>

HSV-1 reactivates most frequently from the trigeminal ganglia, whereas HSV-2 primarily reactivates from sacral ganglia. The rate of reactivation is influenced by the quantity of latent viral DNA in the ganglia. Additionally, type-specific genomic sequences within HSV contribute to differences in recurrence rates at specific anatomical sites.

Host factors also play a critical role in reactivation. Experimental models show that reactivation can be triggered by ultraviolet irradiation, hyperthermia, local trauma, and other physiological stressors—conditions that similarly induce reactivation in humans.

# IMMUNE RESPONSE

Host immunity significantly affects susceptibility to HSV infection, disease severity, and recurrence frequency. The level of cellular immune competence strongly correlates with clinical outcomes.

Individuals with mild impairment in cellular immunity may experience more frequent recurrences and delayed healing of lesions. In contrast, those with severe immunosuppression are at higher risk for disseminated, chronic, or drug-resistant infections.

## <mark>Treatment and Prevention of Scabies</mark>

<mark>There have been numerous reports of the effectiveness of **ivermectin** in the treatment of scabies.</mark> <mark>The usual dosage is $200\ \mu\mathrm{g/kg}$; often, the dose is repeated in 10 to 14 days, although the optimal dosage schedule for scabies has not been definitively established.</mark> <mark>A clinical study comparing ivermectin to topical 5% permethrin showed that a single dose of ivermectin provided a cure rate of 70%, which increased to 95% with a second dose given 2 weeks later.</mark> <mark>In contrast, a single application of permethrin was curative in nearly 98% of patients.</mark> <mark>A topical preparation of 1% ivermectin has shown efficacy in early clinical trials but is not yet commercially available.</mark> <mark>In cases of **crusted scabies**, combination therapy with oral ivermectin and a topical anti-scabicide is commonly used due to the high mite burden, and multiple treatment courses may be necessary to eradicate the infestation.</mark>

## Other Mites

While the scabies mite is the most well-known mite affecting humans, other mites can also cause disease. Mites belong to the class **Arachnida**, order **Acarina** (which includes ticks), and, like scabies mites, are eight-legged organisms with a fused cephalothorax.

Clinically significant mites are generally classified into three suborders: **Trombidiformes**, **Mesostigmata**, and **Sarcoptiformes**. They are often categorized based on their natural host or habitat.

### Follicle Mites

**Demodex** species are common commensals of the human pilosebaceous unit. These mites inhabit hair follicles on the face, scalp, and upper chest. *D. folliculorum hominis* resides within the hair follicle, while *D. brevis* prefers the sebaceous gland infundibulum. The prevalence of **Demodex** infestation increases with age.

<mark>The only oral but highly effective scabicide currently available is **ivermectin**.</mark> <mark>It was discovered in the 1970s from the fermentation broth of the soil actinomycete *Streptomyces avermitilis*.</mark> <mark>Structurally similar to macrolide antibiotics, it lacks antibacterial activity.</mark>

<mark>In mammals, these receptors are primarily located in the central nervous system, and ivermectin normally does not cross the blood-brain barrier.</mark> <mark>However, conditions that compromise the blood-brain barrier may allow CNS entry, increasing the risk of neurotoxicity.</mark>

<mark>Therefore, ivermectin should generally be avoided in children under 5 years of age or weighing less than 15 kg, and during pregnancy or lactation.</mark> <mark>Nonetheless, there are reports of its use in these populations without adverse effects.</mark>

Topical treatment should be applied to all skin areas, including the scalp, groin, navel, external genitalia, finger and toe web spaces, and beneath the nails. It should be applied at night and left in place for 8–12 hours. The skin should be cool and dry before application. A second application is recommended after 7–14 days. Clothing, bedding, towels, and other personal items should be machine washed at 50°C or higher, dry-cleaned, or sealed in a plastic bag for 1 week.

Patients should receive a detailed explanation of their infestation along with clear written information.

The infestation is considered cleared if, 1 week after completion of treatment, there are no signs of active scabies (i.e., no new lesions or nocturnal pruritus). Post-treatment itching may persist for 2–4 weeks.

# Recommended treatments

- <mark>**Permethrin 5% cream**: Apply from head to toe and wash off after 8–12 hours. Repeat treatment after 7–14 days {evidence level Ib; grade A recommendation}.</mark>  
- <mark>**Oral ivermectin**: 200 micrograms/kg, taken with food, given as two doses 1 week apart {evidence level Ib; grade A recommendation}.</mark>  
- **Benzyl benzoate 10–25% lotion**: Apply once daily at night for 2 consecutive days, with re-application after 7 days {evidence level IV; grade C recommendation}.

# Alternative treatments

- **Malathion 0.5% aqueous lotion** {evidence level IV; grade C recommendation}.  
- **Ivermectin 1% lotion**: Reported to be as effective as permethrin 5% cream {evidence level Ib; grade A recommendation}.  
- **Sulphur 6–33%** (as cream, ointment, or lotion): One of the oldest antiscabetic agents. Effective with application on three successive days {evidence level Ib; grade A recommendation}.  
- **Synergized pyrethrins**: Available as a foam in some countries and shown to be as effective as permethrin 5% cream {evidence level IIa; grade B recommendation}.  
- **Lindane**: No longer recommended due to risk of neurotoxicity.

# Crusted scabies

- **Topical scabicide** (permethrin 5% cream or benzyl benzoate 25% lotion): Apply daily for 7 days, then twice weekly until cure, **and**  
- **Oral ivermectin**: 200 micrograms/kg on days 1, 2, and 8.

# <mark>Treatment Recommendations</mark>

- <mark>**Permethrin 5% cream** is effective and requires application on three successive days (level of evidence Ib; grade A recommendation).</mark>  
- <mark>**Synergized pyrethrins**, available as a foam preparation in some countries, are as effective as permethrin 5% cream (level of evidence IIa; grade B recommendation).</mark>  
- **Lindane** is no longer recommended due to its potential to cause neurotoxicity.

# Crusted Scabies

- <mark>Topical scabicide (permethrin 5% cream or benzyl benzoate 25% lotion) applied daily for 7 days, then twice weekly until cure, **and**</mark>  
- <mark>Oral ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg on days 1, 2, and 8.</mark>  
- <mark>For severe cases with persistent live mites on follow-up skin scrapings, additional ivermectin doses may be required on days 9 and 15, or days 9, 15, 22, and 29 (level of evidence IV; grade C recommendation).</mark>

# <mark>Post-Treatment Itch</mark>

Post-treatment itch should be managed with repeated application of emollients. Oral antihistamines and mild topical corticosteroids may also be beneficial.

# Special Situations

- Permethrin is safe to use during pregnancy (level of evidence III; grade B recommendation) and lactation, and is licensed for children aged 2 months and older.  
- Benzyl benzoate and sulfur are considered safe in pregnancy (level of evidence III; grade B recommendation).  
- Ivermectin should not be used during pregnancy or in children weighing less than 15 kg.  
- Malathion has not been studied in pregnant women. Animal studies show no risk, but animal data may not reliably predict human response. Inappropriate use of agricultural-grade malathion for human infestations can cause acute toxicity (level of evidence IV; grade C recommendation).

# Mass Population Treatment (level of evidence Ib; grade A recommendation)

- Recommended for scabies control in endemic areas (e.g., remote communities, displaced populations) and during outbreaks in closed settings such as nursing homes or prisons.  
- All individuals should be treated regardless of symptoms.  
- Oral ivermectin is easier to administer than topical agents, facilitating large-scale treatment.  
- A single dose of oral ivermectin (200 micrograms/kg) is effective.  
- Ivermectin may not sterilize scabies eggs; a second dose after one week improves efficacy. A second dose is recommended (level of evidence Ib; grade A recommendation), though the impact of this on long-term control requires further evaluation.  
- Drug resistance to scabicides, including permethrin and ivermectin, is an emerging concern. The effect of mass treatment programs on resistance development needs further study.

# Follow-Up

A follow-up visit 2 weeks after treatment completion is recommended for microscopy-based test of cure (level of evidence IV; grade C recommendation).

# Partner Management

- Patients should avoid close contact until they and their sexual partners have completed treatment (level of evidence IV; grade C recommendation).  
- Infestation in children is rarely due to sexual abuse and is more commonly from close non-sexual contact.  
- Sexual partners from the past 2 months should be assessed and offered epidemiological treatment (level of evidence IV; grade C recommendation).

# Prevention and Health Promotion

- Risk of scabies can be reduced by limiting the number of sexual partners and practicing strict personal hygiene in crowded environments (e.g., avoiding sharing of underwear, clothing, bedding, and towels; minimizing skin-to-skin contact).  
- Condom use does not prevent transmission.  
- No additional preventive measures have been proven effective.

# Auditable Outcome Measures

- Patients with scabies should be invited for a follow-up visit: target 95%.  
- Suspected scabies cases should receive a recommended treatment regimen: target 95%.

## <mark>Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome</mark>

<mark>Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant cancer predisposition syndrome first described by Peutz (1921) and Jeghers (1949).</mark> <mark>Mucocutaneous pigmentation and intestinal hamartomatous polyposis are hallmarks of the disease.</mark> <mark>The pigmentary lesions resemble those seen in Carney complex, consisting of small hyperpigmented macules that typically appear in childhood (not at birth) on the lips and buccal mucosa.</mark> <mark>These lesions may also involve the eyelids, hands, and feet.</mark>

<mark>The most common malignancies associated with PJS are gastrointestinal, including cancers of the small intestine, colorectum, stomach, and pancreas.</mark> <mark>In addition, nongastrointestinal neoplasms such as breast, cervical, and endocrine tumors (thyroid, testicular, ovarian) are frequently observed.</mark> <mark>More than half of all PJS cases are attributed to mutations in the *STK11* (also known as *LKB1*) gene, a serine/threonine kinase that functions as a tumor suppressor gene.</mark> <mark>Given the high cancer risk, close surveillance of PJS patients is recommended starting at a young age.</mark>

## LEOPARD Syndrome

LEOPARD syndrome (LS) is an autosomal dominant genodermatosis. The acronym LEOPARD stands for:
- **L**entigines
- **E**lectrocardiogram conduction defects
- **O**cular hypertelorism
- **P**ulmonary stenosis
- **A**bnormalities of genitalia
- **R**etardation of growth
- **A**nd sensorineural **D**eafness

Characteristic lentigines usually develop during infancy or early childhood. Clinical diagnosis is based on typical facial features, the presence of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and café-au-lait macules. LS is caused by mutations in the *PTPN11* gene, which encodes the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2, located on chromosome 12. This syndrome is allelic to Noonan syndrome and shares several clinical features with it.

## Other Lentiginosis Syndromes

Other conditions associated with lentigines include:
- Carney complex
- Arterial dissection and lentiginosis
- Laugier-Hunziker disease
- Familial benign lentiginosis
- Bannayan-Ruvalcaba-Riley syndrome (BRRS)
- Centrofacial lentiginosis
- Segmental and agminated lentiginosis

In recent years, genetic loci and causative genes have been identified for Carney complex, PJS, and BRRS.

# Rare Conditions Imitating Rosacea

<mark>Rare conditions that may mimic rosacea include **Morbihan's disease**, which causes persistent lymphoedema and erythema affecting the central and upper regions of the face.</mark> <mark>It can be clinically similar to **Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome**, which also features solid, persistent facial oedema along with recurrent facial nerve palsy and fissured tongue.</mark>

<mark>**Rosacea fulminans**, formerly known as pyoderma faciale or rosacea conglobata, occurs almost exclusively in young women, typically in their 20s and 30s.</mark> <mark>It presents suddenly with intense facial inflammation, including erythema, papules, sterile pustules, coalescing cystic nodules, and draining sinuses.</mark> <mark>Key differential diagnoses include **acne conglobata**, **Gram-negative folliculitis**, and **lupus erythematosus**.</mark> <mark>A **Gram-negative variant of rosacea** has also been reported.</mark>

<mark>**Steroid-induced rosacea** is an under-recognized but important condition, resulting from prolonged systemic or topical glucocorticosteroid use.</mark> <mark>It initially manifests as macular erythema with telangiectasia, progressing later to follicular papules and pustules.</mark> <mark>Discontinuation of steroids is essential, although this may temporarily worsen lesions.</mark> 

<mark>**Granulomatous rosacea** (also called lupoid rosacea) is characterized by reddish-brown papules or nodules appearing alongside diffuse facial erythema.</mark> <mark>Atypical presentations of rosacea may involve persistent erythema in unusual sites such as the scalp or scrotum.</mark>

# Differential Diagnosis Process

<mark>The clinical diagnosis of rosacea relies on patient history, symptoms, skin findings, age, and gender.</mark> <mark>Typical features include **centrofacial erythema**, **telangiectasia**, **papules and pustules**, and **phymatous changes** involving the nose, chin, glabella, and forehead.</mark>

<mark>Features less consistent with rosacea should be evaluated to rule out other conditions:</mark>
- <mark>Extensive scaling (suggestive of seborrhoeic dermatitis or tinea)</mark>
- <mark>Sharply demarcated erythema (as seen in erysipelas)</mark>
- <mark>Widespread scarring</mark>
- <mark>Unilateral inflammation (seen in demodicosis)</mark>
- <mark>Perioral or periorbital inflammation with a narrow non-inflamed zone around orifices (typical of perioral dermatitis)</mark>
- <mark>Marked photosensitivity (seen in lupus erythematosus or polymorphic light eruption)</mark>

<mark>In most cases, diagnosis remains clinical, and skin biopsies are not routinely required.</mark> <mark>However, it is critical not to overlook **angiosarcoma**, which can resemble rosacea in its early stages.</mark> 

<mark>Biopsy with **direct immunofluorescence** is recommended when lupus erythematosus is suspected; comparison with a sample from non-sun-exposed skin helps prevent false-positive results.</mark> 

<mark>Clinicians should consider differential diagnoses such as **lupus erythematosus**, **polymorphic light eruption**, **perioral dermatitis**, **acne**, and the increasingly recognized **mixed facial dermatosis**, which exhibits overlapping features of **seborrhoeic dermatitis** and **rosacea**.</mark>

# Dermatopathology (Skin Biopsy)

Histopathologically, all subtypes of rosacea show:
- **Dilated blood and lymphatic vessels** in the upper and mid-dermis
- **Superficial perivascular and perifollicular mononuclear (lympho-histiocytic) infiltrate**
- Possible **dermal oedema** and **thickened elastic fibres**

In **subtype I (erythematotelangiectatic rosacea)**, histological changes are often minimal.

# Rosacea Therapy and Classification

<mark>Rosacea therapy may include barrier protection practices, topical antimicrobials, oral antibiotics, retinoids, intense pulsed light, and vascular laser modalities for adequate long-term control of symptoms.</mark>

<mark>The Plewig-Kligman classification system describes rosacea progression through stages, with stage III corresponding to phymatous changes.</mark> <mark>In contrast, the National Rosacea Society (NRS) classification states that rosacea does not necessarily progress from one sub-type to another, but that sub-types may overlap in the same individual.</mark> <mark>A provisional grading system was developed by the NRS Expert Committee to standardize clinical assessment.</mark> <mark>Rosacea severity evaluations should also consider the psychological, social, and occupational impact of the condition, as well as individual treatment responsiveness.</mark>

# Epidemiology

<mark>Although the exact prevalence of rosacea is unknown, it is considered common, particularly in Caucasian populations.</mark> <mark>While the majority of cases occur in fair-skinned individuals, rosacea can also affect people of African and Asian descent.</mark> <mark>The NRS estimates that rosacea affects approximately 14 million Americans.</mark> <mark>It occurs in both men and women, with onset typically after age 30.</mark> <mark>However, cases have been reported in children, adolescents, and young adults.</mark>

# <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>

<mark>The clinical variability among rosacea sub-types suggests possible differences in etiology and pathophysiology.</mark> <mark>These may involve facial vascular reactivity, dermal connective tissue structure or composition, extracellular matrix changes, pilosebaceous unit abnormalities, microbial colonization, or a combination of factors that alter the skin’s response to triggers.</mark>

<mark>Rosacea is unmasked or exacerbated by chronic, repeated exposure to triggers—particularly those that induce flushing.</mark> <mark>Common triggers include:</mark>
- <mark>Temperature extremes (hot or cold)</mark>
- <mark>Sunlight</mark>
- Wind
- <mark>Hot beverages</mark>
- <mark>Exercise</mark>
- <mark>Spicy foods</mark>
- Alcohol
- <mark>Emotional stress</mark>
- <mark>Cosmetics and topical irritants</mark>
- <mark>Menopausal flushing</mark>
- <mark>Flushing-inducing medications</mark>

<mark>Flush reactions are mediated by both neural and humoral mechanisms and are typically confined to the face.</mark> <mark>This facial predominance is attributed to higher baseline facial blood flow and a more superficial, extensive cutaneous vascular network compared to other body areas.</mark>

<mark>Histologic studies show dermal matrix degeneration and endothelial damage in rosacea.</mark> <mark>Contributing factors may include increased vascular permeability, impaired clearance of inflammatory mediators, or photodamaged connective tissue altering vascular and lymphatic support in the dermis.</mark> <mark>These changes can lead to chronic inflammation and persistent erythema on facial convexities in susceptible individuals.</mark>

<mark>Sun exposure is considered a contributing factor, though not sufficient alone.</mark> <mark>Solar elastosis is often present in rosacea-affected skin.</mark> <mark>However, rosacea is not more prevalent in outdoor workers, non-facial sun-damaged skin does not develop rosacea features, and photoprovocation studies do not show increased sensitivity to acute UV exposure in rosacea patients.</mark>

<mark>The mechanism of action of oral and topical antimicrobials in rosacea—whether anti-inflammatory or antimicrobial—remains debated.</mark> <mark>The role of commensal microbes such as *Propionibacterium acnes* and *Demodex folliculorum* in triggering folliculocentric inflammation is controversial.</mark> <mark>It is unclear if these organisms directly cause inflammatory papules or if a hypersensitivity reaction to the microbes or associated bacteria (e.g., *Bacillus oleronius*) is involved.</mark>

<mark>Evidence supporting a microbe-driven mechanism in papulopustular rosacea (PPR) includes:</mark>
- <mark>Poor response of rosacea lesions to corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs</mark>
- <mark>Superior efficacy of oral tetracyclines</mark>
- <mark>Effectiveness of benzoyl peroxide in patients who tolerate it</mark>

<mark>It remains uncertain whether clinical improvement in PPR requires a quantitative reduction in *P.</mark> acnes*.

# <mark>Clinical Features</mark>

<mark>**Erythematotelangiectatic rosacea (ETR)** is characterized by:</mark>
- <mark>Persistent facial erythema</mark>
- Flushing
- <mark>Telangiectasia</mark>
- <mark>Central facial edema</mark>
- <mark>Burning and stinging sensations</mark>
- <mark>Skin roughness or scaling</mark>

<mark>These signs and symptoms may occur in various combinations.</mark> <mark>ETR is classified into mild, moderate, and severe sub-types based on clinical presentation.</mark>

# <mark>CLINICAL FEATURES</mark>

<mark>Erythematotelangiectatic rosacea (ETR) is characterized by persistent facial erythema and flushing, telangiectases, central face edema, burning and stinging sensations, skin roughness or scaling, or any combination of these features.</mark> <mark>Mild, moderate, and severe subtypes are recognized.</mark>  

In contrast, papulopustular rosacea (PPR) presents with persistent central facial erythema accompanied by papules and pustules that predominantly affect convex areas of the face. Mild, moderate, and severe forms are also distinguished in this subtype. Burning and stinging occur less frequently in PPR compared to ETR, and flushing tends to be less severe. In both subtypes, facial erythema typically spares the periorbital regions. <mark>Edema may range from mild to severe; when severe, it can manifest as solid facial edema with plaque-like morphology, most commonly on the forehead and glabella, and less frequently on the eyelids and upper cheeks.</mark>

Phymatous rosacea is marked by patulous follicular orifices, thickened skin, nodularities, and irregular surface contours, primarily in convex facial areas. Subtypes range from mild to severe. Rhinophyma (nose involvement) is the most common presentation, but phymatous changes can also occur on the chin (gnathophyma), forehead (metophyma), eyelids (blepharophyma), and ears (otophyma). Women rarely develop phyma, possibly due to hormonal factors, but may exhibit sebaceous hyperplasia with thickened skin and enlarged follicular openings.

Ocular rosacea may precede cutaneous symptoms in up to 20% of cases. In approximately half of patients, eye symptoms follow skin involvement. A minority experience simultaneous onset of ocular and cutaneous manifestations. Importantly, the severity of ocular rosacea does not correlate with the severity of skin disease.

# Environment

<mark>Environmental trigger factors include exposure to extremes of temperature (hot and cold air), temperature changes, caffeine, alcohol, hot and spicy foods, sunlight, exercise, acute psychological stresses, menstruation, demodex mites, and certain medications.</mark> There is controversy regarding whether *H. <mark>pylori* should be considered a trigger factor for rosacea.</mark>

# Cytokines

Due to an impaired permeability barrier in the stratum corneum, the release of various cytokines such as tumour necrosis factor α (TNF-α), IL-1, and IL-6 is triggered, leading to cutaneous inflammation—possibly as an attempt by the epidermis to initiate self-repair. <mark>These pathomechanisms can lead to neurological symptoms such as stinging and burning sensations.</mark>

# Antimicrobial Peptides

Recently, overproduction of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) has been identified as a cause of rosacea lesions. AMPs include defensins and cathelicidins, such as LL-37.

# Toll-like Receptors

Keratinocytes express Toll-like receptors to sense pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) have been shown to be overexpressed in rosacea skin.

# Adaptive Immune Cells

T cells (especially Th1/Th17-polarized immune cells), macrophages, mast cells, and neutrophils are present in all subtypes I–III of rosacea. Neutrophils are assumed to play an essential role in the pathogenesis of rosacea. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) and other proteases produced by neutrophils damage blood vessels, causing inflammation and angiogenesis, which can lead to telangiectasias. Recently, involvement of B cells in the pathomechanism of rosacea has also been demonstrated.

# Mites

Demodex mites, although normally present in adult skin, are found in increased numbers in many rosacea patients. A reduction in Demodex mite density correlates with improvement in rosacea symptoms.

# Blood Vessels

Vascular dilation results in erythema, which may appear transiently as facial flushing. In rosacea, the papillary dermal vasculature is dilated and skin perfusion is increased.

# Nerves

Sensory nerve endings release vasoactive neuropeptides via transient receptor potential (TRP) channels. Two calcium channel blockers and members of the TRP family—transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1)—are of particular interest in rosacea, as they mediate inflammatory responses. These channels are activated by spices, alcohol consumption, and temperature changes. Upon activation, TRPV1 and TRPA1 induce the release of neuropeptides such as pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP), substance P (SP), and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), which collectively cause flushing and erythema through vasodilation. PACAP, SP, and CGRP also promote inflammation by activating mast cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and T cells.

Due to the multifactorial pathogenesis of rosacea, which is difficult to target therapeutically, current treatment strategies focus on symptomatic suppression of inflammation and reduction of disfiguring features. Clinically, four subtypes of rosacea are differentiated based on observable features and severity.

# <mark>Clinical Manifestations and Subtypes of Rosacea</mark>

<mark>Patients with subtype I (erythematotelangiectatic rosacea, ETR) present with centrofacial erythematous macules due to dilated facial capillaries, particularly on the nose and cheeks.</mark> <mark>They may experience episodes of transient erythema (flushing) or non-transient (persistent) erythema.</mark> <mark>ETR flares result from acute vasodilation and innate inflammation.</mark> <mark>With chronic vascular dilation, persistent facial erythema develops.</mark> <mark>Additionally, chronic edema may occur due to extravascular fluid leakage and perivascular inflammation.</mark>
